endorsements.title: Guardrails for GenAI drafted replies in patient portal messaging
endorsements.issuer: Sakr J. npj Digital Medicine 2026;9 (PMID 41942581, doi:10.1038/s41746-026-02621-6)
endorsements.quote: Scoping must therefore be accompanied by interface cues that maintain clinician vigilance regardless of assigned tier.

evidence.title: Assessing Artificial Intelligence-Generated Responses to Urology Patient In-Basket Messages
evidence.outcome: Acceptability of ChatGPT drafted replies to easy versus difficult patient messages
evidence.effect: 56% of responses to easy questions acceptable to send vs 34% for difficult questions (P = .03); easy-question responses were more accurate, complete, helpful, and intelligible.
evidence.quote: ChatGPT performed better on easy questions with 56% of responses to easy questions being acceptable to send as compared to 34% of difficult questions (P = .03).

evidence.title: Opportunities and risks of artificial intelligence in patient portal messaging in primary care
evidence.outcome: Harmful errors or delayed escalation in AI-drafted replies to symptom-related messages
evidence.effect: Two of four erroneous drafts were potentially harmful omissions (blood clot, DKA), which physicians missed in 65% and 75% of cases.
evidence.quote: These erroneous messages were then categorized via team consensus: two were identified as objective inaccuracies, and two were identified as potentially harmful omission (Table 3 ).

evidence.title: Application of AI Chatbot in Responding to Asynchronous Text-Based Messages From Patients With Cancer: Comparative Study
evidence.outcome: Chatbot accuracy, safety and trustworthiness by message scenario (education vs decision-making)
evidence.effect: Education: higher completeness (97.34% vs 93.61%, P=.002), no accuracy/safety difference. Decision-making: lower accuracy and trustworthiness (50.71% vs 93.29% moderately trustworthy or higher, P<.001).
evidence.quote: In the medical decision-making scenario (n=1893), the chatbot exhibited lower accuracy (n=1834, 96.88% vs n=1855, 97.99% for fully accurate responses; P<.001) and trustworthiness (n=860, 50.71% vs n=1766, 93.29% rated as "Moderately trustworthy" or higher; P<.001) compared with physicians.
evidence.sample_unit: deidentified asynchronous text-based medical consultation records

evidence.title: Use of a Medical Communication Framework to Assess the Quality of Generative Artificial Intelligence Replies to Primary Care Patient Portal Messages: Content Analysis
evidence.outcome: Errors in AI-drafted replies to real primary care patient messages, including inappropriate or premature next steps
evidence.effect: 46.3% (93/201) had both strengths and limitations and 27.4% (55/201) had limitations without strengths; only 26.4% (53/201) showed strengths without limitations.
evidence.quote: Overall, 26.4% (53/201) of all messages displayed communication strengths without limitations, 27.4% (55/201) had limitations without strengths, and the remaining 46.3% (93/201) had both.
evidence.sample_unit: GenAI replies to primary care patient portal messages

commentary.bottom_line: One offline study of 100 patient messages found that 56% of ChatGPT drafts to easy questions were acceptable to send versus 34% for difficult questions (P = .03), which suggests draft quality may vary by message class. No study has tested whether limiting drafting to lower-risk classes in live use reduces harmful errors or delayed escalation.

perspectives.view: The single test of the practice is a retrospective rater study of 100 messages with no live deployment. It compared draft quality by question difficulty but did not measure patient outcomes, escalation delays, or how well messages were sorted into tiers. One small, indirect study places certainty at very low.

In a vignette study, physicians missed potentially harmful omissions about a blood clot and DKA in 65% and 75% of cases. Among 201 real primary care drafts, 27.4% had limitations without strengths, including premature next steps. These results suggest clinician review may not catch errors, so scoping may reduce exposure without removing it.

Across 4257 consultation records, chatbot replies in decision-making scenarios were rated moderately trustworthy or higher in 50.71% of cases versus 93.29% for the comparison, while education scenarios showed higher completeness. This suggests message scenario could inform tiering, but no study measured how accurately a live inbox assigns messages to tiers.

The one test of the practice did not report Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy participants. The only study with non-English content came from China and documented the hazard rather than testing scoping. Whether message tiers perform the same way for these patients is unknown.

The endorsing commentary asks that scoping come with interface cues that keep clinicians alert regardless of tier. The missed omissions in simulated review suggest a lower-risk label may not guarantee a safe reply. No study measured whether patients with urgent messages reached a clinician sooner under a scoping policy.

commentary.research_gap: A prospective study in live patient portals should compare scoped versus unscoped drafting and measure misclassification of urgent messages, harmful errors that reach patients, and time to escalation, with deliberate enrollment of safety-net, Medicaid, limited English proficiency, and low-literacy patients.
commentary.underserved_note: The only test of the practice (pmid:39162591) did not report including Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. A hazard study of non-English consultations from China (pmid:40397947) shows the problem exists in that setting but does not show that scoping works there, so any benefit for these groups remains untested.
